young.html: Aristotle wrote two books about words: how to persuade people (the Rhetoric), and how to tell a story that moves them (the Poetics).

When you try to convince someone, Aristotle says, you have three tools. You can show you are someone they can trust (he called this ethos). You can stir their feelings (pathos). Or you can give good reasons (logos). Good speakers use all three.

young.html: About stories, Aristotle said something that sounds simple but is very wise: a good story has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning doesn't need anything before it. The middle follows from the beginning and leads to the end. And the end follows from what came before, with nothing more needed after.

He also loved the moment in a story when everything turns around, like when a character finally learns who someone really is. He called it a reversal and a recognition. When Odysseus comes home in disguise, his old nurse recognizes him by a scar on his leg!

Story arc. Pick a story you know well (a fairy tale, a movie, a book). Draw a line across a page and mark: the beginning, the moment trouble starts, the turning point, the moment someone learns the truth, and the end. Does the ending follow from what came before, or does it come out of nowhere?

full.html: Aristotle's Rhetoric and Poetics (about 335–322 BC) come from his teaching in Athens. Plato's Socrates had attacked rhetoric as flattery and banished most poets from his ideal city. Aristotle takes both seriously, as arts with principles that can be studied.
Rhetoric, he says, is the counterpart of dialectic, the art of argument. Everyone uses both, since everyone sometimes argues, accuses and defends.

full.text: Rhetoric may be defined as the faculty of observing in any given case the available means of persuasion.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. XI, Clarendon Press

full.text: Of the modes of persuasion furnished by the spoken word there are three kinds. The first kind depends on the personal character of the speaker; the second on putting the audience into a certain frame of mind; the third on the proof, or apparent proof, provided by the words of the speech itself.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. XI, Clarendon Press

full.html: A speaker's main proof is the enthymeme, a short argument, like a syllogism with a step left out for the listeners to fill in, and the example, which works like induction. Book II studies the emotions (anger, fear, pity, shame) and the characters of the young, the old and people in their prime, so a speaker can understand an audience. Book III covers style, especially clearness and well-chosen metaphor, and the order of a speech.

Thinking “pathos” is a trick. Aristotle says stirring feelings is fair when the feelings fit the facts; what he objects to is appeals that distract from the question. A judge should not be warped by anger, he says, any more than a carpenter's ruler should be bent.

The Poetics begins with imitation (mimēsis): from childhood we learn by imitating, and we enjoy seeing things imitated well, even things painful to see in life. Then Aristotle defines tragedy: the imitation of a serious, complete action of some size, acted out rather than told, arousing pity and fear and bringing about a catharsis (a cleansing or release) of such feelings. Of its six parts (plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle), plot matters most; he calls it the soul of tragedy.

full.text: Now a whole is that which has beginning, middle, and end. A beginning is that which is not itself necessarily after anything else, and which has naturally something else after it; an end is that which is naturally after something itself, either as its necessary or usual consequent, and with nothing else after it; and a middle, that which is by nature after one thing and has also another after it.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. XI, Clarendon Press

full.html: A good plot hangs together: each event follows from the one before, by necessity or likelihood. That is why, Aristotle says, poetry has a wider truth than history:

full.text: Hence poetry is something more philosophic and of graver import than history, since its statements are of the nature rather of universals, whereas those of history are singulars.
full.author: Aristotle
full.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. XI, Clarendon Press

full.html: The best plots, he says, are complex, with a reversal (peripeteia), when the action turns to its opposite, and a recognition (anagnōrisis), a change from ignorance to knowledge. His favorite example is Sophocles' Oedipus the King, where a messenger comes to cheer the king and instead reveals the truth about his birth.

full.html: The tragic hero should be neither perfectly good nor wicked, but a person like us, of some greatness, who falls into misfortune through some error (hamartia), not through wickedness. That is what makes us feel pity (it is undeserved) and fear (it could happen to someone like us).
The Poetics as we have it covers tragedy and epic. A second book, on comedy, is lost. Umberto Eco's novel The Name of the Rose (1980) imagines a monastery where the last copy survives.

deep.html: Roman teachers like Cicero and Quintilian built on the Rhetoric, and the three appeals are still taught in writing classes. The Poetics was nearly unknown in medieval Europe, but after its rediscovery in the 1500s, critics in Italy and France made strict rules from it, such as the “three unities” of action, time and place, more rigid than anything Aristotle wrote. Today screenwriting books describe plot in terms close to his: beginning, middle and end, rising action and turning points.

Readers still argue about what catharsis means: a purging of pity and fear, a purifying of them, or a clarifying, as we understand the feelings better. Aristotle mentions it only once in the Poetics, without explaining.
